passage:
I think the federal minimum wage should be raised, though perhaps not drastically in a single step.

The current federal minimum of $7.25/hour hasn't changed since 2009, while inflation has eroded its purchasing power by roughly 30%. Someone working full-time at this rate lives below the poverty line in most of America. This seems difficult to justify as a matter of basic fairness—work should provide dignified subsistence.

The standard counterargument about job losses deserves respect but appears overstated empirically. Research on state-level increases and the Seattle minimum wage experiment suggests modest increases cause minimal employment disruption, particularly when phased in gradually. Some job losses may occur, but they're typically modest relative to the gains for millions of workers.

That said, I'm not convinced by arguments for very large jumps (like $20+/hour federally). Regional cost-of-living varies enormously—$15/hour means something different in rural Mississippi than San Francisco. Abrupt large increases do carry real risks of disruption for small businesses and could trigger faster automation.

My view: raise the federal minimum to around $12-13/hour in staged increases over several years, then index it to inflation. This respects that work deserves better compensation than the status quo provides, while avoiding the risks of shock-therapy approaches. States and cities can and should set higher minimums where local conditions warrant.
